medsam-viewer:
Background & Motivation

Radiologists often need to outline an organ across many slices of a 3D CT scan. Repeating that tracing by hand takes time. For SNU’s Creative Integrated Design course with INFINITT Healthcare, our three-person team explored whether a segmentation model could carry a single prompt through the scan.

The Problem

A target that appears in one slice continues through neighboring slices, so outlining each one separately creates repetitive work. At the same time, a useful tool needs to let a radiologist inspect the result in the surrounding anatomy and across the different planes of a scan.

Approach

We extended an open-source PyQt5 DICOM viewer. It loads a DICOM stack, supports HU windowing and 3D reconstruction, and displays axial, sagittal, and coronal views. The user draws a bounding box around the target; MedSAM uses that prompt to segment it across axial slices, and the result appears in all three views for inspection.

One bounding-box prompt guides segmentation across the scan; linked views let the user inspect the result from three directions.

Evaluation & Iteration

The base model struggled with some boundaries in our target organ. I fine-tuned it with LoRA on our CT data; the project comparison showed a 5% improvement in segmentation accuracy for that organ. I also ran PyTorch inference separately from the rendering thread so the viewer could keep responding while segmentation ran.

Outcome & Significance

The course prototype brought prompt-based segmentation and multi-view CT inspection into one viewer, exploring a way to reduce repetitive slice-by-slice tracing. The reported improvement is specific to our target-organ project comparison. The prototype was not clinically validated, so further evaluation would be needed before drawing conclusions about clinical use.
livrecord:
Background & Motivation

Many older adults have memories and experiences they want to pass on, but turning a lifetime of stories into a written autobiography can be difficult. Writing asks people to recall, organize, and put memories into words at the same time. LivRecord began with a simple question: could conversation make it easier to preserve and share those stories?

The Problem

A voice recorder can capture what someone says, but it does not help them discover what to say next or shape separate memories into a story. A fixed list of questions can feel like a form, while a conversation that does not respond to the speaker can lose the thread. We wanted the interaction to invite reflection and follow each person’s memories at a comfortable pace.

Approach

We built Bomi, an AI autobiography coordinator that speaks with the user. Bomi starts with a prompt such as an early memory, listens to the spoken response, and asks a follow-up based on what the person just shared. The speech pipeline combines speech recognition, voice output, and GPT-4-generated follow-up prompts. Responses are brought together as autobiography pages organized by life stage, from childhood to young adulthood; readers can choose a paper background for the pages.

Bomi introduces herself, asks a memory prompt, and records the user’s spoken response. The autobiography is organized by life stage, with a choice of paper backgrounds.

Evaluation & Iteration

We refined question wording and response pacing with older adults so the exchange could leave room for reflection. At the hackathon demo, visitors tried the prototype; some said they wanted to keep talking with Bomi and share more of their stories. These were formative design conversations and informal demo reactions, not a formal study, so they show early interest rather than measured evidence of impact.

Demo: Bomi asks about an early memory, follows up on the response, and turns it into an autobiography page.

Outcome & Significance

LivRecord received the Grand Prize at the KAIST Social Impact Challenge. The prototype showed how a responsive voice conversation could help people begin telling stories that might otherwise remain unwritten, then give those memories a form they could revisit and share. The project’s early reception encouraged us, while further study would be needed to understand how the experience works over longer periods of use.
paranmanjang:
Background & Motivation

I had hundreds of saved articles, but when I sat down to write, I rarely went back to search through them. Paranmanjang (파란만장), a five-person team project, grew from a practical question: could useful reading return to view at the moment it becomes relevant to a draft?

The Problem

Bookmarks sit apart from the writing process. Finding one useful source can mean leaving the draft, searching a long list, and reopening several pages. Recommendations also need to arrive while someone is writing, and saved web pages vary too much in structure to process cleanly without refinement.

Approach

Saving a link starts an ingestion pipeline: the backend extracts and summarizes the page with GPT-3.5, embeds the summary, and stores vectors in Pinecone alongside source metadata in MySQL. While the user writes, the system extracts keywords from the draft, embeds them, and retrieves related saved articles with summaries and source links. I built the editor, recommendation cards, and frontend connections to the saving and retrieval endpoints.

Saved reading is prepared for retrieval, then related sources are surfaced alongside the draft.

The service used FastAPI, MySQL, and Pinecone on Naver Cloud. Docker images were built and deployed through GitHub Actions; the frontend used Next.js, TypeScript, Zustand, and Tailwind CSS, with Google sign-in and Google Docs integration.

Backend services and storage.

Build and deployment pipeline.

Evaluation & Iteration

During implementation, I worked through two practical issues. Web pages differed in structure, so extracting clean article text and filtering unrelated content took repeated adjustment. Recommendations also had to balance query frequency, response time, and relevance while the user was typing. The project materials describe this engineering iteration, but do not report a formal user study or quantitative retrieval benchmark.

Outcome & Significance

The team built and deployed an end-to-end writing tool that brings saved sources and summaries into the drafting workspace. It turns a personal bookmark collection into material that can be rediscovered in context, while keeping source links beside recommendations so writers can return to the original articles. The available project record does not establish whether this changed writing outcomes or saved users time.
upstage-consultation:
Background & Motivation

In a difficult conversation, people may interpret the same messages differently or lack a shared account of what has happened. We explored an AI mediator that could help users reflect on a relationship using the conversation history they provide, rather than relying only on generic advice.

The Problem

A language model can produce confident relationship advice without making clear which details support it. If relevant context is split apart during retrieval, an answer can miss the meaning of a message. We wanted users to see the evidence behind each perspective and check it for themselves.

Approach

We built a Streamlit prototype using Upstage’s Solar model. Users selected an agent, added information about the other person, and uploaded chat history as a CSV or text file. The system summarized personality, relationship patterns, preferences, and contact frequency. Users could then ask a question and compare responses from agents with different perspectives, including The Optimist and The Analyst.

Users provide context and a chat history before asking a relationship question.

The prototype presents two distinct responses alongside its analysis of the uploaded conversation.

Evaluation & Iteration

I found that fixed-size text chunks could split details needed to understand a message. I changed the retrieval pipeline to use semantic chunking, which keeps related sentences together, then combined vector search with keyword matching and reranked the results. Responses linked to excerpts from the uploaded material so users could inspect the basis for each suggestion. The project record does not include a formal user study or quantitative retrieval evaluation, so these changes describe system iteration rather than measured user impact.

Outcome & Significance

The prototype placed in the Top 10 of the Upstage AI Innovation Challenge 2024. It demonstrates a design direction for grounding conversational suggestions in shared evidence and making that evidence visible. Whether this approach improves understanding or outcomes in real interpersonal conflicts remains an open question.
